blocks.text: Mainline Linux gained the two primitives containers need, namespaces (isolated views) and cgroups (resource limits), and LXC combined them into usable system containers before Docker existed.

rows: Added gradually from 2002 (mount) to 2013 (user namespaces, Linux 3.8)
Isolated views: mnt, pid, net, uts, ipc, user, later cgroup, time
Started at Google as "process containers"; merged in Linux 2.6.24 (2008); cgroup v2 unified later
CPU, memory, I/O, PID limits and accounting
Userspace tools to create system containers from namespaces + cgroups

blocks.text: Why LXC wasn't enough for developers

items: System-container model: a whole distro with init, managed like a lightweight VM.
No standard image format, layering or registry for distribution.
Configuration heavy; no build recipe equivalent to a Dockerfile.

blocks.text: Early Docker (2013) used LXC as its execution driver, then replaced it with its own libcontainer (2014), which later became runc.

Q: "What kernel features make containers possible?" A: "Namespaces isolate what a process can see (PIDs, network, mounts, hostname, IPC, users) and cgroups limit what it can use (CPU, memory, I/O, PIDs). LXC combined them first; Docker initially built on LXC, then moved to libcontainer, now runc."

items: Both matured in mainline Linux by ~2013.
LXC = system containers, no image workflow.
